title: The imperative and stressed pronouns
subtitle: Prends ! Asseyez-vous ! C'est à moi.
summary: Give instructions and advice with the imperative, use moi, toi, lui... after prepositions, place adverbs, ask with qu'est-ce qui, and talk about unspecified quantities.

lesson.heading: The imperative
lesson.note: Take the *tu*, *nous* and *vous* forms of the present and drop the subject. Verbs in **-er** lose the **-s** of the *tu* form: *tu parles* → **Parle !**

lesson.heading: Irregular and reflexive imperatives
lesson.note: With a reflexive verb, the pronoun comes after the verb with a hyphen, and *te* becomes **toi**.

lesson.heading: Pronouns and the negative imperative
lesson.text: In a positive order, the pronoun follows the verb: **Donne-moi**, **Donne-lui**, **Donne-nous**, **Donne-leur**. In a negative order, put **ne ... pas** around the verb and the pronoun goes back in front, in its normal form (*toi* → **te**).

examples.note: Give me the address of a good doctor!

lesson.note: The imperative can sound abrupt. It's normal for instructions (a recipe, a gym class) or to encourage someone, but to ask a favour say **Est-ce que vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?** rather than *Répétez !*

lesson.heading: Stressed pronouns: moi, toi, lui ...
lesson.text: The stressed pronouns are **moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles**. Use them after a preposition (*chez, avec, pour, sans* ...) and after **c'est ... qui**. To say who something belongs to, use **être à** + a pronoun or a name.

examples.text: C'est **pour lui**. Je viens **avec toi**. Ils partent **sans eux**.
examples.note: It's for him. I'm coming with you. They're leaving without them.

examples.text: Tu peux aller **chez lui** en toute confiance.
examples.note: You can go to him (to his practice) with complete confidence.
I'm the one organising the conference.

examples.text: — À qui est ce livre ? — Il est **à moi** !
examples.note: Whose book is this? - It's mine!

examples.text: Ce verre est à Isabelle ? — Non, il est **à Fabienne**.
examples.note: Is this Isabelle's glass? - No, it's Fabienne's.

lesson.heading: Adverbs and how strong an adjective is
lesson.text: With a verb in the present, an adverb usually goes **right after the verb**. To make an adjective weaker or stronger, put **un peu**, **assez**, **très** or **extrêmement** in front of it.

examples.note: She speaks slowly. He understands quickly.

examples.text: **un peu** fatiguée < **assez** fatiguée < fatiguée < **très** fatiguée < **extrêmement** fatiguée
examples.note: a bit tired < quite tired < tired < very tired < extremely tired

left.label: Qu'est-ce qui = what (subject)
left.text: The *thing* is the subject: the verb follows directly.

right.label: Qu'est-ce que = what (object)
right.text: The thing is the object: a subject (*tu, vous* ...) follows *que*.

lesson.heading: Some: du, de la, de l' → pas de
lesson.text: For an amount you don't count, use **du** (masculine), **de la** (feminine) or **de l'** before a vowel or silent *h*. In the negative, all of them become **pas de** (**pas d'** before a vowel).

examples.text: Il mange **de la** soupe, **du** fromage, **du** pain.
Elle ne mange **pas de** soupe, **pas de** pain.
examples.note: She doesn't eat any soup or bread.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb with its tu imperative.
Vous pouvez faire ce travail ? → ___ ce travail !
Tu peux t'occuper des enfants ? → ___ des enfants !
exercises.explanation: Reflexive imperative: **Occupe-toi !** - no *-s*, and *te* becomes *toi* after the verb.

exercises.prompt: Vous pouvez vous asseoir ? → Which is the imperative?

options: Ne toi occupe pas du chien !
exercises.explanation: In the negative the pronoun goes back before the verb as **te** (**t'**): *Ne t'occupe pas*.

exercises.prompt: Make it negative: *Donnez-lui l'adresse !* ("Don't give him the address!")
Je vais chez mes amis, je vais chez ___.
Ce document est pour Louise et Émilie ? — Non, ce n'est pas pour ___.
exercises.explanation: Two women → **elles**. *Leur* is never used after a preposition.

exercises.prompt: Monsieur, ce livre est à vous ? — Oui, il est à ___.
Put the adverb in the right place: "He often goes to the cinema."
exercises.explanation: In the present, the adverb goes **right after the verb**.

exercises.prompt: *La machine ne marche pas.* Which question asks about it?
options: Qui est-ce que ne marche pas ?
exercises.explanation: The thing is the subject of *marche*, so use **qu'est-ce qui**.

exercises.statement: Elle ne mange pas de la soupe.
exercises.explanation: In the negative, *de la* becomes **de**: *Elle ne mange **pas de** soupe.*
